And they think, "This is amazing. I just need to generate calls." Not so fast. Before you send a single call, you need to understand exactly what the campaign accepts. What locations, what schedule, what type of caller, what services, what traffic sources, what qualification requirements. What's the billable event? Are there caps? Are there duplicate rules? Because a $300 campaign isn't worth much to you if most of your traffic doesn't qualify. In this episode, I'm going to show you how to read a Papercall campaign from top-to-bottom and how technology can automatically enforce many of these rules before the call ever reaches the buyer. Think of a Papercall campaign as a set of instructions. The campaign tells you what the buyer wants, where they want it, when they want it, how much they're willing to pay, and what has to happen before you get paid. A typical campaign might include campaign name, vertical, payout, billable event, geographic coverage, schedule, qualification requirements, traffic source restrictions, call duration or AI qualification rules, daily caps, concurrency, duplicate rules, and routing requirements. Every one of these settings can affect whether your call makes money. So, let's break them down. The first thing I want to look at is not just the payout. I want to know what triggers the payout. We learned this in episode 5. Maybe it's a qualified call. Maybe it's CPQ. Maybe it's an appointment. Maybe it's an acquisition. Maybe it's a sale. Imagine two campaigns. Campaign A pays $150 for a qualified call. Campaign B pays $800 for an acquisition. You cannot compare those numbers directly. The $800 campaign may require you to generate many opportunities before one acquisition occurs. Always read the payout together with the billable event. Those two numbers belong together. Next, where does the buyer actually want calls? A campaign might be nationwide. It might accept only certain states. It could target specific cities. Or it could go all the way down to individual zip codes. This matters enormously. Imagine you're generating plumbing calls nationwide, but one buyer only covers South Florida. A customer calls from Dallas. Great consumer, great intent, wrong geography. If that's your only buyer, you may have nowhere to send that call. This is why publishers want broad coverage. And it's why networks often combine multiple buyers to create larger geographic footprints. In ProNexus.ai, routing can use geographic information such as zip code, state, and campaign coverage to determine which eligible buyer can receive the opportunity. Instead of the publisher manually figuring out where every call should go, the routing technology can make that decision dynamically. Geography isn't the only thing that matters. Time matters, too. Maybe a buyer accepts calls Monday through Friday from 9:00 to 5:00. But your website doesn't stop generating traffic at 5:00. Customers search at night. They search on weekends. They call whenever they need help. So, what happens when the buyer is closed? A basic setup might simply reject the call. But that opportunity still has value. A better system can look for another available buyer. And if no live buyer is available, technology can potentially capture the consumer's information, schedule an appointment, or convert that opportunity into another monetizable event. This is something we focus heavily on inside ProNexus.ai. Don't automatically assume an unanswered or unroutable call has zero value. There may be another way to monetize the opportunity. Now, let's look at qualification requirements. This is where campaigns can become very different, even inside the same vertical. Two roofing buyers might both purchase roofing calls, but want completely different customers. One may accept roof repair and replacement. Another may want replacement only. One might accept homeowners and commercial properties. Another might require residential homeowners. One may have additional requirements around the project. This is why you need to read every qualification rule carefully. And once again, AI can help. In ProNexus, conversational AI can analyze what the caller actually says and compare those signals against the campaign requirements. Instead of looking only at call duration, we're trying to understand, did this caller actually meet the requirements of this specific campaign? Here's one publishers sometimes overlook. What traffic sources does the campaign allow? A buyer may accept Google search, SEO, organic websites, certain paid media, or approved publisher sources. But they may restrict other sources. Some buyers may not accept traffic from Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, incentivized traffic, or certain call center models. That doesn't necessarily mean a traffic source is universally bad. It means the buyer decides what they're willing to purchase. This is exactly why we talked earlier about sub IDs and separate tracking numbers. If you have five traffic sources, don't throw all five into one bucket. Track them separately. In ProAcsys, the goal is to let networks identify those sources and use that information when determining which campaigns and buyers are eligible for the call. That protects your good traffic when one source has a problem. Next, you'll often see something like 60 seconds, 90 seconds, 120 seconds. That's the traditional call duration requirement we discussed in episode 4. But now you know why duration alone can be imperfect. A legitimate customer might complete the important part of the conversation in 70 seconds. Another caller might stay connected for 4 minutes without meeting the campaign requirements. That's why in proacsys.ai, we designed AI Verdict Trademark to add another layer of intelligence. The system can analyze the conversation against the campaign's rules. Was there legitimate intent? Was the requested service correct? Did the caller appear to meet the qualification requirements? What actually happened? Duration is still useful, but now we can combine the clock with an understanding of the conversation. Now let's talk about caps. A buyer might say, "I want 20 calls per day." Once they receive 20, they're done. That's the daily cap. Here's the problem for a publisher. Your traffic doesn't necessarily stop when the buyer reaches their cap. Your ads are still running. Your websites are still ranking. Customers are still calling. This is another reason having multiple buyers is so important. If buyer A reaches their cap, the routing system should be able to look for buyer B, then buyer C, then another eligible destination. The more coverage and buyer depth you have, the better chance you have of monetizing the traffic you're already generating. This is one of the major advantages of building a network rather than depending on a single buyer. There's another campaign setting beginners often don't understand, concurrency. Concurrency means how many calls a buyer can handle at the same time. Imagine a buyer says, "I can accept 50 calls per day." That sounds great. But they only have two agents answering phones. If five calls arrive simultaneously, they may not be able to handle all five. That's where concurrency limits become important. Maybe that buyer can receive only two active calls at a time. When those lines are occupied, new calls need another destination. A routing platform like ProNexus can consider availability and routing rules before determining where the next call should go. Because sending a valuable call to someone who can't answer it doesn't help the publisher, the buyer, or the customer. Next, duplicates. Suppose the same customer calls today and then calls again tomorrow. Should the buyer pay twice? Maybe. Maybe not. That's determined by the campaign's duplicate rules. A campaign might define a duplicate window such as 7 days, 14 days, 30 days, or another period. So, when you see a campaign payout, check the duplicate policy. This can materially affect your revenue. And technology can automatically compare the caller against previous activity instead of expecting somebody to manually inspect thousands of calls. Again, campaign rules aren't just text on a page. They should become logic inside the platform. Now things get really interesting. Imagine you have three buyers that can all accept the same roofing call. Buyer A pays $150. Buyer B pays 200. Buyer C pays 250. Should you always send the call to buyer C? Not necessarily. Maybe buyer C doesn't cover that zip code. Maybe they've reached their daily cap. Maybe they're currently at maximum concurrency. Maybe they don't accept that traffic source. Maybe they're closed. So, routing isn't simply who pays the most. It's who is eligible to receive this specific call right now. And among those eligible destinations, which routing logic should apply? That's what modern pay-per-call technology is designed to solve. In Pro Axess, the goal is to evaluate those conditions automatically and route each opportunity according to the campaign and buyer rules. Now, here's something I'm particularly passionate about. What happens when nobody can take the call? Traditional thinking says, "No buyer, no revenue, dead call." But think about what you actually have. You may have a real consumer, a real phone number, a service they're looking for, geographic information, and strong purchase intent. Why should that opportunity simply disappear? Inside Pro Axess.ai, we're building around the idea that an unroutable or unanswered call can potentially be recovered. The system can capture the available information, use AI to understand what the consumer needs, and depending on the setup, turn that opportunity into a lead, an appointment, or another monetizable event. We call this concept call recovery because publishers already paid to create that opportunity. If technology can recover even a percentage of those otherwise lost calls, that can directly improve publisher economics. Now, let's put everything together. When you're creating or evaluating a campaign, don't think of it as simply roofing $200. Think about the complete rule set. What event triggers payment? What geography is accepted? What schedule? What qualifications? Which traffic sources? What duration or AI verification rules, what daily cap, what concurrency, what duplicate window. Which buyers can receive the traffic? And what happens if the first buyer can't take the call? In a basic call tracking system, many of these pieces may need to be configured and managed separately. What we're building with ProAxi.ai is a system where these campaign rules can work together across tracking, routing, AI analysis, publishers, buyers, leads, appointments, and billing. Because every additional opportunity you successfully route or recover can potentially mean more revenue from traffic you've already generated. So, here's the lesson I want you to remember from episode six. Never choose a campaign based only on the payout. A $300 payout with poor coverage, restrictive qualifications, limited hours, and low buyer capacity might be less profitable for your traffic than a lower paying campaign with excellent coverage and strong availability. Read the entire campaign. Understand the billable event. Understand the geography. Understand the traffic restrictions. Understand the caps. Understand the routing. And most importantly, understand what happens to your traffic when the perfect buyer isn't available. That's one of the reasons we're building ProAxi.ai the way we are. The goal isn't simply to track calls. The goal is to help you monetize more of the opportunities you're already generating. Because in performance marketing, improving your profit doesn't always mean generating more traffic. Sometimes it means losing less of the traffic you already paid for. And in the next episode, we're going to take the next step and look at how calls are actually routed between publishers, networks, and buyers. 👉 Hear how Mo built a pay per call company on pace for $1M+ this year, mistakes included

📞 Want help building your brokerage? Watch this VSL: https://middlemanmafia.io/?cx=Gt7hIKJ

In this video: Interview with Mo, owner of True Ring Leads, who left his SMMA for pay per call in final expense. Licensed insurance agent since 2022. I started by buying leads with my mom's credit card, learned to run my own ads, and now run AgentCalls, a pay per call brokerage selling calls and leads to insurance agents. Through Middleman Mafia I teach people how to build their own pay per call business

📲 Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/ceohec
💬 Telegram: https://t.me/theceohec

Results vary. Nothing here is a guarantee of income. Figures mentioned are my own or my students' and aren't typical.

metadata.title: My Pay Per Call Biz is Boring, But it Makes Me $10M/year
metadata.author: John Ventura
metadata.shortDescription:
How Agents Are Making $50,000 Per Month Only Taking Calls: http://theagentsystem.net?utm_source=yt&video=KeC4mKXnzs4

The NEW Way to Buy Qualified Calls in 2026: https://youtu.be/UFWPlbDFPOg

---------------------------------------------------------------

Pay per call made me over $10 million in a single year and the business behind it is embarrassingly boring

Most people are chasing AI automation agencies and trendy business models that burn out in 6 months. Meanwhile boring businesses like pay per call quietly print money because they solve a problem every company on the planet already pays for: customers

I'm breaking down exactly how pay per call works, the middleman model that Amazon, Uber, and Airbnb all used to build billion-dollar empires, and how you can start the same thing from zero

You'll see the actual math on how 50 calls per day at $15 in margin turns into $750 in daily profit and how the system handles 500 calls without any extra work

I'm also walking through the mistake I made for years in affiliate marketing that kept me stuck, the two massive exits that changed how I think about building businesses, and the 5 steps for starting a pay per call business from scratch

This isn't dropshipping. It's not SMMA. It's a boring, defensible, scalable business that prints while you sleep

CHAPTERS:
00:00 - $10M/Year From a Boring Business?
01:02 - Amazon, Uber, Airbnb Are All Middlemen
02:11 - Pay Per Call Explained in 60 Seconds
02:55 - The Math That Changes Everything
04:00 - Why Agencies Hit a Ceiling
04:49 - The Mistake That Kept Me Stuck
06:04 - Two Exits That Rewired My Brain
06:49 - Inside My Three Companies Today
07:51 - Why This Isn't the Next Trend
09:00 - Where Most People Blow It Up
09:46 - 5 Steps To Start From Zero

metadata.title: What is the Process of Mass Tort Litigation? Attorney Joe Lyon Explains
metadata.author: Attorney Joseph Lyon
metadata.shortDescription:
To learn more about your legal rights and the resources available to help you pursue justice in a personal injury case, visit thelyonfirm.com and call 800.513.2403 for a free consultation.

"A lot of people confuse the term class action with the term mass tort. The cases that involve injuries from pharmaceutical products are properly classified as mass tort. There are some similarities with class actions, but they are not class actions in the traditional sense. From my perspective, this is a very good thing. We are able to consolidate our cases for the purposes of discovery, which allows us to work in conjunction with firms around the country who are dealing with the same or similar issues. This creates efficiencies within the system that allow individuals to move forward against some of the most powerful companies in the world. Without the ability to consolidate, we would be expending tremendous amounts of resources on one individual case, and the economics of that system may not justify moving forward. 

But, from a practical sense, we often get asked the question, "what can I expect from my case as we move forward with the consolidation process with cases from around the country?" The most common format  for consolidation is through what's called multi-district litigation, or an MDL. When your case is accepted by my firm and we move forward through the MDL process, the first thing we will ask you to do is to complete what's called a plaintiff fact sheet. A plaintiff fact sheet is a very concise form of discovery that's going to ask such as, "when did you first take the medication?" "how long did you take the medication?" "when did you first have the side effect being claimed in the litigation?" "what doctors prescribed the medication? and "what doctors treated you for the respective injuries?" Typically the plaintiff fact sheet doesn't go into a lot more detail than that because the parties are trying to gather and compile information that is the same or similar across the broad spectrum of all the plaintiffs in the case. When you have thousands of cases pending it's important to simply try to categorize the cases in order to understand where the similarities or dissimilarities may lie. 

Once the plaintiff fact sheet has been submitted there's also medical authorizations that will need to be completed for the defendants. My firm will, at that point, have gathered most of the critical medical records in order to substantiate the case, but the defendants will also have the opportunity to review and gather that evidence themselves.

Once that information has been exchanged, the process moves forward into what's called a bellwether selection process. The bellwether process allows the courts and the lawyers to select particular cases from the broader pool of litigation for the purposes of understanding what the value may be of the case where the strengths and the weaknesses of both the defendants and the plaintiffs cases may lie. It's done in an effort to try to hopefully come up with some sort of value of what the global resolution may look like, and hopefully to come to some finality in the case. 

When cases are consolidated it's important to understand certain aspects of the litigation. While your case may not be presented directly before the judge, certain questions of science that are ruled upon may impact your case. The process is known as a Daubert hearing or Daubert process, but this scientific hearing and scientific inquiry, typically on whether the particular drug can cause a particular disease, the answer to that question will typically dictate whether the individual case will move forward, or whether the litigation as a whole may be dismissed.

Once the primary questions of science are answered through the court, which apply globally to the litigation, the next step is to select certain cases for trial. Those cases are designed to be representative of the broad pool of cases in the litigation so that the attorneys for both sides, and the court, can have a better sense of what is representative of this mass tort as a whole. 

To go back to the original question, you know, "is my case a class action or a mass tort?" There are a lot of similarities between the two, due to the immense volume of cases surrounding the litigation. In the common, we refer to these as common questions of law that overlap between many of the cases in the litigation.

That being said, your case is ultimately, your case. The injuries that you suffered are unique to you. How these injuries have impacted you life and your family are unique to you, the amount of money that has been lost through lost wages or through your medical expenses; those are questions that are unique to you and will be worked up individually. If the settlement process is unsuccessful, my firm is in a position to push the case forward and to ultimately pursue your day in court as an individual, and not part of a class action."

segments.text: What if the medication you trusted, the
product you used, or the water you drank
every day
was the very thing making you sick? For
thousands of Americans, this isn't just
bad luck, it's corporate negligence.
But when one company harms thousands of
people, how do you actually fight back?
Here's exactly what happens when you
file a mass tort lawsuit step-by-step,
from the moment you're injured to the
day your case enters federal court.
Every mass tort begins with someone
getting hurt. It could be a defective
implant failing in your body,
years of using a weed killer like
Roundup now linked to cancer,
or a prescription drug like Suboxone,
Ozempic, or Depo-Provera causing side
effects no one warned you about.
At first, it feels like it's just you.
But news reports, FDA warnings, or
ongoing lawsuits reveal the bigger
picture. Thousands of others are
suffering for the exact same reason.
That's when you know, this isn't an
isolated incident. It's part of a much
larger fight. The next step is reaching
out to a mass tort attorney. These
lawyers specialize in cases involving
dangerous drugs, toxic exposure, and
defective products.
They review your medical history, your
timeline of exposure, your symptoms, and
your damages, from medical costs to lost
wage. If your case lines up with
hundreds or even thousands of others,
you qualify to join the litigation.
You're not just signing up for a list,
you're hiring someone to represent your
individual case every step of the way.
Once you're in, your attorney starts
building your case from the ground up.
They'll collect everything. Your medical
records, prescriptions, diagnostic
reports, test results, even workplace
exposure records. They work with medical
experts and scientists to link your harm
to the company's product or conduct. The
goal is simple, prove your injuries
weren't random. They were caused by
corporate negligence.
After your evidence is in place, your
lawyer files your lawsuit in court. This
is your case with your name, your
injuries, and your claim for
compensation.
At the same time, hundreds or even
thousands of similar lawsuits are being
filed across the country. All pointing
at the same company. All telling a
similar story.
That's when the federal court system
steps in organizing the fight.
When so many lawsuits target the same
defendant, the courts often combine them
into something called multi-district
litigation or MDL. Your case doesn't
disappear.
It isn't merged with others.
Instead, it's transferred to one federal
judge who oversees all the pre-trial
work for every case at once.
This process keeps things efficient.
Lawyers share evidence and expert
witnesses.
There's one set of rulings on motions.
It prevents duplicate work and
conflicting outcomes.
But most importantly, your case stays
your case.
Your injuries, your damages, your day in
court.
Once in the MDL, discovery begins.
Uncovering corporate documents, studies,
emails, depositions, and scientific
evidence. Plaintiff attorneys nationwide
collaborate, pooling resources to expose
the truth and strengthen each case.
The scale of the MDL gives you access to

videos.full_text: What if the medication you trusted, the product you used, or the water you drank every day was the very thing making you sick? For thousands of Americans, this isn't just bad luck, it's corporate negligence. But when one company harms thousands of people, how do you actually fight back? Here's exactly what happens when you file a mass tort lawsuit step-by-step, from the moment you're injured to the day your case enters federal court. Every mass tort begins with someone getting hurt. It could be a defective implant failing in your body, years of using a weed killer like Roundup now linked to cancer, or a prescription drug like Suboxone, Ozempic, or Depo-Provera causing side effects no one warned you about. At first, it feels like it's just you. But news reports, FDA warnings, or ongoing lawsuits reveal the bigger picture. Thousands of others are suffering for the exact same reason. That's when you know, this isn't an isolated incident. It's part of a much larger fight. The next step is reaching out to a mass tort attorney. These lawyers specialize in cases involving dangerous drugs, toxic exposure, and defective products. They review your medical history, your timeline of exposure, your symptoms, and your damages, from medical costs to lost wage. If your case lines up with hundreds or even thousands of others, you qualify to join the litigation. You're not just signing up for a list, you're hiring someone to represent your individual case every step of the way. Once you're in, your attorney starts building your case from the ground up. They'll collect everything. Your medical records, prescriptions, diagnostic reports, test results, even workplace exposure records. They work with medical experts and scientists to link your harm to the company's product or conduct. The goal is simple, prove your injuries weren't random. They were caused by corporate negligence. After your evidence is in place, your lawyer files your lawsuit in court. This is your case with your name, your injuries, and your claim for compensation. At the same time, hundreds or even thousands of similar lawsuits are being filed across the country. All pointing at the same company. All telling a similar story. That's when the federal court system steps in organizing the fight. When so many lawsuits target the same defendant, the courts often combine them into something called multi-district litigation or MDL. Your case doesn't disappear. It isn't merged with others. Instead, it's transferred to one federal judge who oversees all the pre-trial work for every case at once. This process keeps things efficient. Lawyers share evidence and expert witnesses. There's one set of rulings on motions. It prevents duplicate work and conflicting outcomes. But most importantly, your case stays your case. Your injuries, your damages, your day in court. Once in the MDL, discovery begins. Uncovering corporate documents, studies, emails, depositions, and scientific evidence. Plaintiff attorneys nationwide collaborate, pooling resources to expose the truth and strengthen each case. The scale of the MDL gives you access to far more evidence and legal firepower than any single case ever could. Before every case moves forward, a few are chosen for bellwether trials. Early test cases. These trials help gauge how juries react to the evidence, how strong the arguments are, and what the cases might be worth. Often, the results drive settlement negotiations for the remaining plaintiffs, saving years of litigation while still allowing individual outcomes. After bellwether results, most mass tort cases are resolved through settlements. But if no fair deal is reached, your case can go to trial on its own. Unlike a class action, your compensation is calculated based on your unique damages, your medical costs, your suffering, your lost income, not averaged across thousands. Filing a mass tort lawsuit isn't fast, it's complex, but it's one of the most powerful tools for holding corporations accountable while ensuring every victim's voice and every loss is recognized. Because when profits cause pain, mass torts make justice possible one case at a time.

metadata.title: How the Money Works in Pay Per Call | Billing, Payouts, Margins & Profit- Pay Per Call University #8
metadata.author: ExclusiveLiveCall
metadata.shortDescription:
How does the money actually move through a Pay Per Call business?
In Episode 8 of Pay Per Call University, we break down the financial side of the industry — from buyer billing and publisher payouts to margins, disputes, cash flow, recovery, and real profitability.
A buyer might pay $200 for a call, but that does not mean you made $200.
You need to understand:
- Buyer revenue
- Publisher payout
- Network spread
- Telecom and technology costs
- Payment processing
- Prepaid balances
- Auto-recharge
- Postpaid buyers
- Credit limits
- Publisher payment terms
- Cash-flow timing
- Billable vs. non-billable calls
- Credits and disputes
- AI-assisted call classification
- Profit per call
- Recovering missed opportunities
One of the biggest lessons in this episode is simple:
Revenue is not profit.
A network can process a huge amount of volume and still have poor economics if payouts, technology costs, disputes, payment failures, and overhead consume the margin.
We also explain how ProAxis.ai is designed to help connect billing, routing, call intelligence, recovery, and performance data instead of treating them as separate systems.
AI Voice Recovery
One of the most important examples is a missed call.
If a buyer cannot answer, that opportunity does not necessarily have to disappear.
With ProAxis AI Voice Recovery, AI can take the missed call and attempt to book the consumer directly with the buyer.
There is no upfront recovery fee just to have the feature available.
If the buyer answers the call normally, there is no recovery charge.
If AI takes the call but does not successfully book an appointment, there is no $5 appointment-recovery charge.
Only when AI successfully recovers the missed call and books the appointment do we charge $5 for that recovered call.
The appointment can then appear in the buyer's Google Calendar and in the built-in calendar available through ProAxis.
That leads to another major lesson:
Making more profit doesn't always mean generating more traffic. Sometimes it means losing fewer of the opportunities you already generated.
This episode also starts opening the door to the much larger performance marketing ecosystem we'll be covering next.
In upcoming episodes, we'll learn how to:
- Find Pay Per Call buyers
- Onboard buyers
- Recruit publishers
- Generate traffic
- Build nationwide buyer coverage
- Use Call RTB and Ping-based routing
- Build lead forms
- Use Lead Ping/Post and RTB
- Generate consent certificates
- Use CRM to manage buyers, publishers and networks
- Use Market Intelligence
- Work with intent data and lead enrichment
- Use Outreach AI
- Build automated email, SMS and AI Voice workflows
- Buy and sell call traffic inside a larger ecosystem
Pay Per Call University is free to watch.
The goal is not simply to teach you what Pay Per Call is.
The goal is to help you understand how to build a real performance marketing business around measurable outcomes.
🌐 ProAxis.ai
Key lesson from Episode 8:
Don't ask only how much revenue you generated. Ask how much profitable, collectible revenue you actually kept — and how much value your technology helped you recover.

metadata.title: How Pay Per Call Routing Actually Works | RTB, Overflow & AI Call Recovery | Pay Per Call Episode #7
metadata.author: ExclusiveLiveCall
metadata.shortDescription:
What actually happens after a consumer calls a Pay Per Call tracking number?
In Episode 7 of Pay Per Call University, we go behind the scenes and break down the full routing process — from the moment the consumer dials the number to the moment the call reaches the right buyer.
You’ll learn how modern Pay Per Call routing works, including:
- Tracking numbers and source attribution
- Campaign identification
- ZIP code and geographic routing
- IVR vs. conversational AI
- Building an eligible buyer pool
- Buyer priority and payout logic
- Caps and concurrency
- Traffic-source restrictions
- Real-Time Bidding (RTB)
- Ping-based RTB
- Overflow routing
- Buyer no-answer handling
- AI receptionist
- Appointment scheduling
- Call Recovery
- Turning missed calls into leads
- AI Verdict™ after the conversation
One of the most important lessons in this episode is that call routing is not simply forwarding one phone number to another.
A real routing engine has to decide:
Who is eligible? Who is available? Who has capacity? Who accepts the source? Who is willing to pay? And what happens if nobody answers?
We also explain how ping-based RTB can work without manually assigning every downstream buyer a fixed phone number. Instead, a platform can ping an external network or demand partner, receive a bid and routing instructions, and then route the call in real time.
Inside ProAxis.ai, our goal is to take call routing beyond traditional forwarding.
We combine routing with RTB, AI Voice, overflow, appointments, Call Recovery, AI Verdict™, buyer rules, campaign logic, and billing so more of the opportunities you generate have a chance to monetize.
Because in Pay Per Call, the goal is not simply to generate more calls.
The goal is to lose fewer good opportunities.
And as you continue through Pay Per Call University, we’ll show you how ProAxis can also help you build and operate your own network, manage publishers and buyers, use lead forms and lead RTB, automate outreach, recover missed opportunities, and grow inside a larger performance marketing ecosystem.
🌐 ProAxis.ai
Key lesson from Episode 7:
Generating the opportunity is only half the battle. What your routing technology does with that opportunity determines how much value you capture.
#PayPerCall #PayPerCallUniversity #ProAxis #CallRouting #RTB #LeadGeneration #PerformanceMarketing #AffiliateMarketing #AI #CallTracking #VoiceAI

You found the buyers. You built the campaigns.
Now there’s one big question:
Who is going to generate the traffic?
In Episode 11 of Pay Per Call University, we move to the supply side and learn how to find Pay Per Call publishers, build relationships with them, and give good publishers a reason to send traffic to your network.
We cover:
- Where to find Pay Per Call publishers
- Telegram and Pay Per Call communities
- Networking events like Contact.io, LeadsCon, Affiliate Summit East & West
- Google Ads, SEO, affiliates, call centers and other networks as traffic sources
- Why publishers care about more than just payout
- Why nationwide coverage can attract more publishers
- How to start publishers with controlled tests
- Why payment terms and cash flow matter
- Using CRM to properly manage publisher relationships
- Why traffic-source quality and transparency matter
- Sub-publishers and source separation
- How reputation can make or break your network
One of the biggest lessons in this episode is simple:
If you gave your word, honor it.
If a publisher delivered legitimate billable traffic and your agreement says they should be paid on a certain date — pay them on time.
Performance marketing is a relatively close-knit industry. Publishers talk. Networks talk. Buyers talk.
Your good name can become one of the most valuable assets in your business.
We’ll also look at how ProAxis.ai can help you operate your own network by managing publishers, campaigns, traffic relationships, CRM, tracking, routing and more.

videos.full_text: Welcome back to PaperCall University. Over the last few episodes, we've started turning everything we've learned into an actual business. In episode 9, we learned how to find buyers. We created demand. In episode 10, we learned how to take that demand, create campaigns, connect buyers, establish routing and billing rules, and get ready to receive traffic. But, there's still one pretty important problem. Who's going to make the phone ring? You can have amazing buyers. You can have great payouts. You can have incredible technology. You can have AI, RTB, routing, tracking, and beautiful dashboards. But, if nobody is generating traffic, nothing happens. That's where publishers come in. Today, I'm going to teach you how to find publishers, what publishers actually care about, how to approach them, how to build long-term relationships with them, and why your reputation can eventually become one of the most valuable assets in your entire business. Let's build the supply side. Let's quickly refresh something we covered earlier. A publisher is a person or company responsible for generating the consumer opportunity. That consumer might come from Google Ads, SEO, >> [music] >> websites, Google Maps and local search, social media, native advertising, email, call centers, affiliate traffic, or many other permitted traffic sources. The publisher creates or captures the consumer demand. Your network connects that opportunity with buyer demand. And when the agreed performance event occurs, the publisher gets paid. Think about our business like this. Buyers equal sign demand, publishers equal sign supply. You need both. Without buyers, you have nobody to monetize the traffic with. Without publishers, you have no traffic to monetize. >> [music] >> Your job is to build the bridge between the two. When I say publisher, don't imagine one specific type of company. A publisher could be one person sitting at home running Google Ads. It could be an SEO company controlling hundreds of websites. It could be an agency, a media buyer, a local search operator, an affiliate marketer, a call center, another paper call network, or a large publisher operating multiple traffic sources and dozens of sub publishers underneath them. One publisher might send you five calls a day. Another publisher might send you 500. And here's something really important. The size of the publisher doesn't automatically determine the quality of the traffic. What matters is where the traffic comes from, whether it complies with your campaign requirements, whether the consumers have legitimate intent, and ultimately whether your buyers can successfully monetize it. Here's something I want you to understand before you start recruiting publishers. Good publishers have choices. Imagine someone can generate 500 qualified roofing calls every month. You're probably not the only network that wants those calls. So, don't approach publisher recruitment with this attitude, "I have a campaign. Send me traffic." Why should they? Ask yourself. Why should this publisher send their valuable traffic to ME? >> [music] >> Maybe you have better coverage. Maybe you have competitive payouts. Maybe you pay reliably. Maybe you have more stable campaigns. Maybe your technology is easier to work with. Maybe your reporting is better. >> [music] >> Maybe you communicate better. Maybe you can monetize opportunities that another network can't. Publisher recruitment is a competitive business. You need to give good publishers a reason to choose you. One of the biggest mistakes beginners make is assuming publishers only care about payout. Of course, payout matters, but the biggest number on the screen doesn't necessarily make the publisher the most money. Let's say network A offers $200 per qualified roofing call. Sounds amazing. But they have extremely limited coverage and can only monetize 10% of your legitimate traffic. Another network pays $150 per qualified call, but they have significantly broader coverage. Now, which network actually makes the publisher more money? You can't answer that just by looking at the payout. You need to look at the entire monetization opportunity. That's why publishers care about things like payout [music] plus coverage plus conversion plus stability plus caps plus payment reliability. Don't just compete on the number. >> [music] >> Compete on the business opportunity. This is exactly why we spent so much time talking about building buyer coverage. Imagine I'm an SEO publisher. I own websites generating roofing calls across 30 states. Do I really want to maintain relationships with 15 different networks just because each network can only monetize a few zip codes? Probably not. If I can find a reliable network with strong coverage, [music] competitive economics, and good technology, that's extremely attractive. And now you can see how the business starts connecting together. >> [music] >> More buyers create more demand. More demand creates better coverage. Better coverage attracts better publishers. Better publishers create more traffic. More traffic attracts more buyers. And now you have a flywheel. Buyers, coverage, publishers, traffic. More buyers. That's how our network starts growing. There's another thing I want you to remember. Publishers aren't magically creating traffic for free. Google Ads costs money. Media costs money. Websites costs money. SEO costs money. Content costs money. Employees costs money. Call center agents costs money. Data costs money. Technology costs money. A publisher may spend money today to generate the traffic they're sending you while waiting days or weeks for you to pay them. That means when a publisher sends you traffic on payment terms, they are extending trust to your business. And this brings us to one of the most important lessons I'm going to teach you in this entire course. I want to stop here for a minute because this isn't really a pay-per-call lesson. This is business 101. When you close a deal with a publisher or another network, >> [music] >> you're probably going to have agreements in place. You might have an MSA, master services agreement. You might have an IO, insertion order. Those documents can define the campaign, pricing, payment [music] terms, and other responsibilities. Let's say you agreed to payment terms under which traffic from a particular billing period will be paid on an agreed future date. Whatever payment schedule you agreed to, honor it. If the traffic was delivered, if it met the agreed billing requirements, if the invoice is legitimate and the payment is due, pay them. Don't suddenly change the agreement. Don't disappear. Don't make people chase you for money they've already earned. You gave your word. You received the traffic. The traffic was billable. Honor your commitment. And here's what some network owners don't understand. They think, "If I delay paying this publisher, I keep more cash in my bank account." Okay. But what did that actually cost you? Imagine that publisher was sending you 20 profitable billable calls every day. You don't pay them when promised. What happens? They stop sending you traffic. Yesterday, [music] 20 calls. Today, zero. Maybe you protected some cash temporarily, but you just shut off a source producing future revenue and potentially future profit. And good publishers usually have other options. If another network pays them reliably and you don't, what do you think they're going to send tomorrow's traffic? Not to you. Paying publishers on time isn't simply the right thing to do. It can be fundamental to the economics of your business. But losing one publisher isn't even the biggest problem. The bigger problem is your name. I'm from Israel, and we have an old biblical saying, "A good name is better than precious oil." And I think that's an incredible lesson for business. Thousands of years ago, precious oil represented something extremely valuable. But the message is still relevant today. Your good name can be worth more than money. Performance marketing is a niche industry compared with the enormous world of digital marketing. Eventually, everybody knows everybody. Publishers talk, networks talk, buyers talk, people meet at conferences, people communicate in industry groups. Someone asks, "Have you worked with these guys?" And somebody answers, "Yes, great company. They always pay us on time." That answer is worth money. Or the answer, "Be careful. We had problems getting paid." That answer can cost you money. Your reputation follows you, and this can create a network effect in the wrong direction. You don't pay one publisher, they tell another publisher. Someone mentions it to another network. People start asking questions. Eventually, your name becomes associated with, "They don't pay." >> [music] >> And now, people may refuse to work with you before you've even spoken with them. I've seen this industry from both sides. We have publishers and networks approach us wanting to work together, and we don't accept everybody. There are publishers we may choose not to work with because there are serious concerns about their traffic. Poor quality, fake or manipulated traffic, incentivized traffic where it isn't permitted, or other quality issues. And there are networks we may choose not to work with because there are serious concerns about whether they honor their payment commitments. Maybe other people in the industry were left financially hurt. So, reputation matters on both sides. Publishers need a reputation for delivering quality. Networks need a reputation for paying what they owe. Don't be the person everyone warns everybody else about. Here's the rule. You gave your word, you received the traffic, it was billable according to your agreement, >> [music] >> payment is due. Pay it on time. Obviously, legitimate disputes happen. That's business. Maybe the traffic violated campaign requirements. Maybe there were duplicates. Maybe there was fraud. Maybe calls were outside the approved geography. That's why we have agreements, campaign rules, recordings, reporting, AI analysis, and reconciliation. But, don't manufacture disputes because you're having a bad cash flow week. Your publisher shouldn't finance mistakes you made somewhere else in your company. Manage your cash flow. Know what you owe. Know when you owe it. Maintain sufficient reserves. And honor your agreements. Because in performance marketing, your word is part of your product. And this brings me to something inside Prolaxis.AI that goes far beyond simply routing calls. CRM. metadata.author: Tristan Ahumada
metadata.shortDescription:
MAJOR FCC Text Message Rules Update: What Marketers Need to Know | TCPA Changes Delayed to 2026

Big news for businesses dealing with text message marketing laws and TCPA compliance updates! The FCC has just announced a crucial postponement of new text message opt-in rules and marketing consent requirements until January 2026. This delay comes after the Insurance Marketing Coalition lawsuit challenged the FCC text message consent regulations, forcing a review of these new FCC regulations that would have dramatically impacted text message marketing guidelines.

The delay provides relief for those struggling with text marketing compliance, especially regarding business compliance TCPA standards. Small business TCPA rules were particularly concerning, as many feared the original 2025 deadline would create significant challenges. These text message marketing regulations have sparked intense debate about marketing regulations 2025 implementation, with multiple stakeholders raising concerns about the FCC regulatory changes.

Filing - https://tcpaworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/ORDER-POSTPONING-EFFECTIVE-DATE-OF-ONE-TO_ONE.pdf

Google Doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wGQfTVOwR0lMDApd6CbkHb9EgrPBOa2NwW3L9QXuCYQ/edit?usp=sharing

Why Your Google Ads Are Getting Clicks But No Calls (And What To Do About It)

This is something that I see/hear pretty often when it comes to Google Ads.

Spending thousands of dollars on ad spend, only to end up with nothing in return.

Video description:

In this video you’ll learn more about pay per lead (PPL) model for restoration companies. This training will help you make a decision as to whether PPL is worth it for your restoration company or not. 

We’ll go over how PPL works, how much are water damage leads, and the comparison between PPL and marketing agency services. 

How Pay Per Lead for Water Damage Works?

It works exactly as you may think. You partner up with a lead generation company and you start receiving leads from them (usually calls), paying only for billable leads. 

What determines a billable lead?

It depends on the deal you have with the lead generation company. Some companies bill you based on call duration, while others bill you based on the intent of the caller. 

How Much Are Water Damage Leads?

Water damage leads usually go from $200 on the lower end up to $1,000 on the higher end. 

Pricing will vary per zip code, with leads from metro areas like Los Angeles, Houston, and Miami usually coming at the highest price. 

If you’ve ran Google Ads (PPC) advertising before, you’ll notice that one water damage lead equates to 5-10 clicks from PPC. Cost per click in your area is one of the biggest factors that determine the cost of a lead.

To continue learning, watch this video!

metadata.author: FFL Success Zone | Integrity Connect Inbounds
metadata.shortDescription:
In this Integrity Connect inbound call training, we break down exactly how one agent went from zero to writing $10,000 in production from just 19 inbound calls.
Melissa shares her story of transitioning from healthcare IT (non‑sales background) into life insurance sales, and how she mastered inbound calls by focusing on script discipline, pacing, and rapport.
We also walk through a full live inbound call breakdown so you can hear exactly how top agents:

Build trust quickly on inbound calls
Stay in control without sounding scripted
Handle “I thought it was free” objections
Avoid quoting price too early
Use silence and pacing to increase close rate
Keep calls simple and follow the script
Close consistently without pressure

What you’ll learn:

How to master the inbound life insurance script
Why slowing down increases your close rate
How to handle inbound objections naturally
How to build rapport even as an introvert
Why not rushing the call changes everything
The exact framework behind high RPC (Revenue Per Call)

This is a must‑watch for any life insurance agent working inbound calls through Integrity Connect, Ringba, or ILC, and for agents who want to improve their closing consistency and confidence.
If you’re struggling with inbound calls, this video shows you exactly what to fix and how to win.

metadata.title: 📞 How to Always Get Back on Script | Inbound Final Expense Insurance Calls
metadata.author: FFL Success Zone | Integrity Connect Inbounds
metadata.shortDescription:
In this inbound call training, we break down how life insurance agents can always get back on script—no matter what the inbound caller says. If you’re taking inbound life insurance calls from Integrity Connect or final expense and Medicare traffic, this video is required viewing.
Inbound life insurance calls can derail fast from initial objections, off‑topic stories, competition shopping. However, top producers know how to regain control and guide the conversation back to the script without sounding robotic or pushy. This training shows you how.
You’ll learn:

How to reset control on inbound final expense insurance calls
Why sticking to your script increases close rate and compliance
How Family First Life inbound traffic behaves compared to outbound leads
The exact mindset and transitions top FFL agents use
How to lead inbound callers while building trust

Whether you sell final expense, term life, whole life, or mortgage protection, mastering script control on inbound calls will dramatically improve conversions.
If you’re a life insurance agent running inbound calls, this video will help you sell more policies with less resistance.

metadata.title: TCPA Compliance for Insurance Agents: What You Need to Know in 2026
metadata.author: Henson Legal
metadata.shortDescription:
Insurance agents: TCPA violations can cost you $500-$1,500 per call. One agent spent $220,000 to settle. Here's how to stay compliant without slowing down your business.                                                                                                                    
  
In this webinar hosted by Accelerated Automation, TCPA attorney John Henson breaks down exactly what insurance agents and agencies need to know about calling, texting, AI voice, lead vendors, and do-not-call compliance in 2026.
                                                                                                                                                 
  WHAT WE COVER:                                            
  00:00 - Introduction & why TCPA matters for insurance agents
  02:30 - The two buckets: regulated technology vs. DNC rules                                                                                    
  05:15 - Automated dialers, ringless voicemail & AI voice requirements                                                                          
  08:40 - Texting rules: calls and texts are treated the same                                                                                    
  10:20 - Do Not Call list, EBRs & the 90-day/18-month rules                                                                                     
  15:00 - Opt-out requirements: the 7 magic words                                                                                                
  19:30 - Can you still send informational texts after an opt-out?                                                                               
  23:00 - Lead vendors: what to check before you buy leads                                                                                       
  28:00 - Consent language: what actually protects you                                                                                           
  32:00 - The one-to-one consent rule (effective Jan 27, 2026)                                                                                   
  36:00 - List hygiene: DNC scrubbing, reassigned numbers & repeat litigators                                                                    
  40:00 - AI voice and automated messaging: what the FCC requires                                                                                
  45:00 - Practical compliance checklist for insurance agents                                                                                    
  50:00 - Q&A                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                 
                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
  ABOUT THE SPEAKERS:                                                                                                                            John Henson is a TCPA compliance attorney and founder of Henson Legal PLLC. Former General Counsel at ConsumerAffairs and VP of Compliance at LendingTree. He advises insurance agencies, lead generation companies, AI voice platforms, and real estate tech companies on telemarketing compliance.                                               
                                                                                                                                                 
  Mariah Gates is the CEO of @AcceleratedAutomation2023, a technology consulting firm serving insurance agents.                                      
  
  📧 Contact: john@henson-legal.com                                                                                                              
  🔗 Website: https://henson-legal.com                      
  💼 LinkedIn: www.linkedin.com/in/john-h-henson/
